reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design - Part 2: Ground investigation and testing
chapter_title: Laboratory tests on soil and rock

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The laboratory test programme is set with the rest of the ground investigation programme (Section 2), and field test and sounding results should guide the choice of test samples (2.4.1.3).
sections.body: (1)P The laboratory test programme shall be set up together with the other parts of the ground investigation programme (see Section 2). (2) Wherever possible, field test and sounding results should be used to choose the test samples (see 2.4.1.3). (p. 60)
key_points: Set the laboratory programme with the rest of the investigation (p. 60).
Use field tests and soundings to choose test samples (p. 60).
sections.applicability: Overview and roadmap for the whole of Section 5 and its supporting Annexes L-W.

sections.summary: Heading for the general requirements for laboratory tests: general (5.2.1), procedures, equipment and presentation (5.2.2) and evaluation (5.2.3).
sections.body: Heading for 5.2.1 to 5.2.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 60)

sections.title: General requirements
sections.summary: The Section 5 requirements are a minimum; further specifications, presentation or interpretation may be needed for the ground or the aspects of interest, and the tests needed for design parameters are specified.
sections.body: (1) The requirements of this section should be taken as a minimum. (2) Additional specifications, presentation or interpretation suited to the ground or the geotechnical aspects of interest may be required. (3)P Details of the tests needed for the design parameters shall be specified. (p. 60)
key_points: Section 5 requirements are a minimum (p. 60).
Specify the tests needed for design parameters (p. 60).

sections.title: Procedures, equipment and presentation
sections.summary: Tests follow existing EN and EN ISO documents, or alternatives meeting this standard; equipment is checked as adequate and calibrated and its reliability compared with comparable soils or rocks; methods and deviations are reported; classification results are plotted with the soil profile.
sections.body: (1)P Tests shall be done and reported per existing EN and EN ISO documents. NOTE: CEN ISO/TS documents exist for several laboratory tests and some EN ISO documents are in preparation. (2) Alternative methods and procedures may be chosen if this standard's requirements are met. (3)P Laboratory equipment shall be checked as adequate, fit for purpose, calibrated and within calibration requirements. (4) Reliability of equipment and procedures should be checked against data on comparable soil or rock types. (5)P Methods and procedures shall be reported with the results, and deviations from a standard procedure reported and justified. (6) Where appropriate, soil classification results should be presented with the soil profile on a plot summarising the description and all classification results. (7) If possible and required, the positions of other tests (e.g. oedometer, triaxial) should be shown on the same plot. (p. 60)
key_points: Tests per existing EN and EN ISO documents (p. 60).
Equipment adequate, calibrated and within calibration requirements (p. 60).
Report methods and justify deviations (p. 60).
Plot classification results with the soil profile (p. 60).
sections.applicability: Baseline requirements applicable to every laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Evaluation follows 6.3; individual results are compared with others to rule out contradictions and checked against literature values, index property correlations and comparable experience.
sections.body: (1) Evaluation requirements are in 6.3 (p. 60). (2) Individual results should be compared with other results to check the data do not contradict each other. (3) Results should be checked against literature values, correlations with index properties and comparable experience (p. 61). (pp. 60 to 61)
key_points: Evaluation requirements are in 6.3 (p. 60).
Check results against each other, literature, index correlations and experience (p. 61).

sections.summary: Heading for preparation of soil specimens for testing: objective (5.3.1) and requirements (5.3.2).

sections.applicability: Governs specimen preparation for every soil laboratory test described later in Section 5.

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: Soil specimen preparation aims at specimens as representative as possible of the sampled soil; five specimen types: disturbed, undisturbed, re-compacted, remoulded and reconstituted.
sections.body: (1) Preparation aims at test specimens as representative as possible of the soil sampled. (2) Five specimen types may be distinguished: disturbed, undisturbed, re-compacted, remoulded and reconstituted. (p. 61)
key_points: Five specimen types: disturbed, undisturbed, re-compacted, remoulded, reconstituted (p. 61).

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Heading for soil specimen requirements: quantity of soil (5.3.2.1) and handling and processing (5.3.2.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.3.2.1 and 5.3.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 61)
sections.applicability: Governs specimen preparation for every soil laboratory test described later in Section 5.

sections.title: Quantity of soil
sections.summary: Specimens must be large enough for the largest particles present in significant quantity and for natural features such as structure and fabric; Annex L gives minimum masses.
sections.body: (1)P The specimen shall be large enough for the largest particle size present in significant quantity and for natural features such as structure and fabric (e.g. discontinuities). NOTE: Annex L gives minimum masses of disturbed soil for classification and re-compacted tests and the masses needed to prepare undisturbed specimens for strength and compressibility tests. (p. 61)
key_points: Specimen size suits the largest particles and the soil fabric (p. 61).
Annex L gives minimum soil masses (p. 61).
sections.applicability: Governs specimen preparation for every soil laboratory test described later in Section 5.

sections.title: Handling and processing
sections.summary: Samples follow EN ISO 22475-1, are clearly labelled, protected from damage, deterioration and temperature change, kept from drying where moisture loss matters, prepared under controlled humidity, disaggregated without breaking particles and subdivided without segregation.
sections.body: (1)P EN ISO 22475-1 shall be observed. (2)P All samples shall be labelled clearly and unambiguously. (3)P Samples shall be protected at all times from damage, deterioration and excessive temperature change; undisturbed samples need special care against distortion and water loss in preparation; container material shall not react with the soil. (4)P Soil shall not dry before testing if moisture loss can affect results. (5) Undisturbed samples should be prepared under controlled humidity and protected from water content change if preparation stops. (6)P Disaggregation shall not break individual particles; any special treatment of bonded or cemented soil shall be specified. (7)P Subdivision shall give representative portions without segregation of large particles. (p. 61)
key_points: Label samples clearly; protect from damage and temperature change (p. 61).
No drying before testing where moisture loss affects results (p. 61).
Disaggregate without breaking particles; subdivide without segregation (p. 61).

sections.title: Preparation of rock specimens for testing
sections.summary: Heading for preparation of rock specimens for testing: objective (5.4.1) and requirements (5.4.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.4.1 and 5.4.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 62)

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: Rock specimen preparation aims at specimens as representative as possible of the rock formation; Annexes T to W and X.2 give more detail and guidelines.
sections.body: (1) Preparation aims at specimens as representative as possible of the rock formation. NOTE: Annexes T to W and X.2 give more detail on preparing rock specimens and some guidelines. (p. 62)
key_points: Annexes T to W and X.2 detail rock specimen preparation (p. 62).
sections.applicability: Governs specimen preparation for every rock laboratory test described later in Section 5 (classification, swelling, strength).

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Preparation is specified (storage, moisture condition, coring method, tolerance checks) and reported; measuring instruments are checked regularly; water content changes are avoided or counteracted; records give source, orientation, dates, dimensions, water contents, drying, description, sketch or photo, core recovery and RQD, and tolerance data.
sections.body: (1)P How a rock specimen is prepared shall be specified; where that cannot be met, it shall be prepared as near the specification as possible and the actual preparation reported. (2)P Instruments for straightness, flatness and perpendicularity of end surfaces shall be checked on a registered regular basis, with tolerances meeting at least the specific test requirements. (3)P To be specified: storage conditions (short and/or long term), the specimen moisture condition at test, the core preparation method and the method of checking dimension and shape tolerances. (4)P Changes in water content should be avoided; where the natural water content changes, its effect shall be counteracted in preparation if relevant. (5) The cause and effect of any water content change should be reported. (6)P The need for re-coring to a set dimension shall be defined with reference to laboratory coring method, coolant and re-saturation. (7) To be recorded and reported with the results: specimen source with depth or level and orientation; dates of preparation and testing; comments on representativeness; all dimension and shape measurements and conformity; water content as received, in preparation and saturated; drying conditions (air or oven, pressurised or partial vacuum). (8) For interpretation: a physical description including rock type (e.g. sandstone, limestone, granite), structural features, discontinuities and inclusions or non-homogeneities; a sketch or colour photograph except for monotonous homogeneous rock; core recovery and RQD where possible (p. 62); and data supporting the tolerance checks on the right cylindrical form, end flatness and end perpendicularity to the core axis (p. 63). (pp. 62 to 63)
key_points: Specify storage, moisture condition, coring and tolerance checks (p. 62).
Avoid water content changes; counteract and report them (p. 62).
Record source, orientation, dimensions, water contents and drying (p. 62).
Give description, sketch or photo, core recovery and RQD (p. 62).

sections.title: Tests for classification, identification and description of soil
sections.summary: Heading for soil classification, identification and description tests: general (5.5.1) and requirements (5.5.2), water content, bulk density, particle density, particle size, consistency limits, density index, dispersibility and frost susceptibility (5.5.3 to 5.5.10).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.1 to 5.5.10; it has no text of its own. (p. 63)
sections.applicability: Routine soil classification, identification and description testing in the laboratory, the basis for every other soil test.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Soil classification, identification and description follow EN ISO 14688-1 and EN ISO 14688-2; Annex M gives test details, interpretation and minimum numbers of samples and tests per stratum.
sections.body: (1)P Classification, identification and description of soil shall follow EN ISO 14688-1 and EN ISO 14688-2. NOTE: Annex M gives more on the individual tests and their interpretation and a guideline for the minimum number of samples and tests in one stratum. (p. 63)
key_points: Classify and describe soil per EN ISO 14688-1 and -2 (p. 63).
Annex M gives minimum numbers of tests per stratum (p. 63).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Requirements for all classification tests
sections.summary: For all classification tests, the oven-drying temperature is chosen with care, since too high a temperature can harm the measured value.
sections.body: (1) For all classification tests, special care should be taken in choosing the oven-drying temperature, as too high a temperature can harm the measured value. (p. 63)
key_points: Choose oven-drying temperature with care (p. 63).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Water content determination
sections.summary: Heading for water content determination: objective and requirements (5.5.3.1) and evaluation (5.5.3.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.3.1 and 5.5.3.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 63)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Water content is the ratio of the mass of free water to the mass of dry soil, measured on specimens of at least Quality Class 3 and on each soil type in a mixed sample (CEN ISO/TS 17892-1, X.4.1.2).
sections.body: (1) The test determines the water content of soil, the ratio of the mass of free water to the mass of dry soil. (2) Specimens should be at least Quality Class 3 (3.4). (3) Where a sample holds more than one soil type, water contents should be found on specimens of each. NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-1 (X.4.1.2). (p. 63)
key_points: Water content = mass of free water / mass of dry soil (p. 63).
Specimens at least Quality Class 3 (p. 63).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Evaluation allows for gypsum, highly organic soil, pore water with dissolved solids and closed water-filled pores, and checks how far as-received values represent in-situ ones; for such soils drying at about 50 °C may suit better than the usual (105 ± 5) °C, with caution.
sections.body: (1)P Significant gypsum, highly organic soil, pore water containing dissolved solids and soil with closed water-filled pores shall be allowed for where relevant. (2) How far the laboratory value on soil as received represents the in-situ value should be checked, allowing for sampling method, transport and handling, specimen preparation and laboratory environment. (3) For the soils in (1)P, drying at about 50 °C may suit better than the usual (105 ± 5) °C, but the results should be treated with caution. (p. 63)
key_points: Allow for gypsum, organic soil, dissolved solids and closed pores (p. 63).
Check as-received water content against in-situ (p. 63).
About 50 °C drying may suit such soils instead of (105 ± 5) °C (p. 63).

sections.title: Bulk density determination
sections.summary: Heading for bulk density determination: objective and requirements (5.5.4.1) and evaluation and use (5.5.4.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.4.1 and 5.5.4.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 64)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: The test gives the bulk (total) mass density of soil including liquid and gas, on specimens of at least Quality Class 2, by a specified method (CEN ISO/TS 17892-2, X.4.1.3).
sections.body: (1) The test determines the bulk (total) mass density of soil, including any liquid or gas. (2) Specimens should be at least Quality Class 2 (3.4). (3)P The test method shall be specified. NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-2 (X.4.1.3). (p. 64)
key_points: Bulk density on specimens of at least Quality Class 2 (p. 64).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: Evaluation considers sample disturbance; laboratory density of coarse soil is generally approximate unless special sampling is used; bulk density serves design actions from soil, processing other tests and, with water content, dry density.
sections.body: (1) Evaluation should consider possible sample disturbance. (2) Except with special sampling methods, the laboratory density of coarse soil is generally only approximate. (3) Bulk density can be used for design values of actions from soil and in processing other laboratory tests. (4) It can also serve other soil characteristics, e.g. with water content to compute dry density. (p. 64)
key_points: Laboratory density of coarse soil is generally approximate (p. 64).
Bulk density serves design actions and, with water content, dry density (p. 64).

sections.title: Particle density determination
sections.summary: Heading for particle density determination: objective and requirements (5.5.5.1) and evaluation (5.5.5.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.5.1 and 5.5.5.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 64)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: The test determines by a conventional method the density of solid soil particles, choosing the method for the soil type (CEN ISO/TS 17892-3, X.4.1.4).
sections.body: (1) The test determines by a conventional method the density of the solid particles. (2)P The method shall be chosen for the soil type. NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-3 (X.4.1.4). (p. 64)
key_points: Particle density method chosen for the soil type (p. 64).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Particle densities outside the normally expected (2 500 to 2 800) kg/m3 call for a check of mineralogy, organic matter and geological origin.
sections.body: (1)P If a stratum's measured particle densities fall outside the normally expected (2 500 to 2 800) kg/m3, the mineralogy, organic matter and geological origin shall be checked. (p. 64)
key_points: Normal particle density range (2 500 to 2 800) kg/m3 (p. 64).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Particle size analysis
sections.summary: Heading for particle size analysis: objective and requirements (5.5.6.1) and evaluation and use (5.5.6.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.6.1 and 5.5.6.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 64)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Particle size analysis gives mass percentages of size ranges: sieving above 63 µm and hydrometer or pipette sedimentation at or below 63 µm, or calibrated equivalents; fine soil is not dried before sedimentation, and organics, salts and carbonates are removed or corrected for where suitable.
sections.body: (1) The test determines the mass percentage of each particle size range (p. 64); NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-4 (X.4.1.5). (2)P Two methods shall be used by particle size: sieving for particles > 63 µm (or the closest sieve) and sedimentation by hydrometer or pipette for particles ≤ 63 µm (or the closest sieve). (3) Equivalent methods calibrated against these two may be used. (4)P Fine soil specimens shall not be dried before sedimentation. (5) Removal of organics, salts and carbonates before sieving and sedimentation, or corrections for them, should be used where suitable; NOTE: carbonates and organic matter can cement or coagulate and affect the distribution. (6) For some soils, e.g. chalky soil, carbonate removal is unsuitable (p. 65). (pp. 64 to 65)
key_points: Sieve above 63 µm; hydrometer or pipette sedimentation at or below 63 µm (p. 65).
Do not dry fine soil before sedimentation (p. 65).
Carbonate removal is unsuitable for chalky soil (p. 65).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: The report states drying method, removal of organics, salts and carbonates, carbonate or organic content and the mass basis; Dn is the size with n % finer by weight, D10, D30 and D60 give uniformity and curvature coefficients, and D15 and D85 serve filter criteria.
sections.body: (1)P The report shall state the drying method; whether organics, salts and carbonates were removed and how; the carbonate and/or organic content if relevant; and whether mass fractions refer to the total mass (including carbonate and organic matter). (2) The size with n % of particles by weight smaller is Dn; D10, D30 and D60 can give the coefficients of uniformity and curvature. (3) D15 and D85 can be used in soil filter criteria. (p. 65)
key_points: Report drying method and any removal of organics, salts, carbonates (p. 65).
D10, D30, D60 give uniformity and curvature coefficients (p. 65).
D15 and D85 for filter criteria (p. 65).

sections.title: Consistency limits determination
sections.summary: Heading for consistency limits determination: objective and requirements (5.5.7.1) and evaluation and use (5.5.7.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.7.1 and 5.5.7.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 65)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Consistency (Atterberg) limits cover liquid, plastic and shrinkage limits; only liquid and plastic limits are covered. The liquid limit method (fall cone or Casagrande) is specified, the fall cone preferred; specimens are at least Quality Class 4 to characterise in-situ soil.
sections.body: (1) The consistency (Atterberg) limits are the liquid, plastic and shrinkage limits; only the liquid and plastic limits are covered. (2) They characterise how clays and silty soil behave as water content changes, and mainly drive their classification. (3)P The liquid limit method (fall cone or Casagrande apparatus) shall be specified (p. 65). (4) The fall cone should generally be preferred, being more reliable, particularly for low plasticity soil. (5) Specimens should be at least Quality Class 4 (3.4) if results are to characterise the soil in situ. NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-12 (X.4.1.6) (p. 66). (pp. 65 to 66)
key_points: Only liquid and plastic limits are covered (p. 65).
Specify fall cone or Casagrande; fall cone preferred (p. 66).
At least Quality Class 4 to characterise in-situ soil (p. 66).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of results
sections.summary: Liquid and plastic limits correlate with properties such as compressibility or optimum water content; Ip serves classification and strength correlations; IC (or IL) with water content gives consistency; IA from Ip and clay percentage serves classification and correlations.
sections.body: (1) Properties such as compressibility or optimum water content can be derived by correlation with the liquid or plastic limit. (2) The plasticity index Ip, from liquid and plastic limits, can be used in classification and in correlations, e.g. with strength. (3) The consistency index IC (or liquidity index IL), from the limits and the current water content, can represent consistency and enter correlations. (4) The activity index IA, from Ip and the percentage of clay particles, can be used in classification and correlations, e.g. with strength. (p. 66)
key_points: Ip from liquid and plastic limits for classification and correlations (p. 66).
IC or IL from limits and current water content (p. 66).
IA from Ip and clay particle percentage (p. 66).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Determination of the density index of granular soil
sections.summary: Heading for determination of the density index of granular soil: objective and requirements (5.5.8.1) and evaluation and use (5.5.8.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.8.1 and 5.5.8.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 66)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: The density index relates void ratio to standard laboratory reference values and indicates compaction of free-draining granular soil; tested soil should have less than 10 % fines (passing 0,063 mm) and less than 10 % gravel (retained on 2 mm); results are reported with grading, water content and particle density.
sections.body: (1) The density index relates a sample's void ratio to reference values from standard laboratory procedures and indicates the compaction state of a free-draining granular soil. (2)P Quantity and quality of samples, test procedure and preparation of each specimen shall be specified or checked. (3) The soil should contain less than 10 % fines (passing the 0,063 mm sieve) and less than 10 % gravel (retained on the 2 mm sieve). (4)P Results shall be reported with the particle size analysis, natural water content, particle density and oversize percentage (if applicable); deviations from (3) shall be reported. NOTE: see X.4.1.7. (p. 66)
key_points: Density index indicates compaction of free-draining granular soil (p. 66).
Less than 10 % fines (0,063 mm) and less than 10 % gravel (2 mm) (p. 66).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: Laboratory maximum and minimum densities are not necessarily limiting densities and vary widely; the density index can characterise shear strength and compressibility of coarse soil.
sections.body: (1) Laboratory maximum and minimum densities do not necessarily represent limiting densities, and these tests are generally recognised as highly variable. (2) The density index can characterise shear strength and compressibility of coarse soil. (p. 67)
key_points: Laboratory max and min densities are not necessarily limiting, and vary (p. 67).
Density index characterises strength and compressibility of coarse soil (p. 67).

sections.title: Soil dispersibility determination
sections.summary: Heading for soil dispersibility determination: objective (5.5.9.1) and requirements (5.5.9.2).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.9.1 and 5.5.9.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 67)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: Dispersibility tests identify dispersive clayey soils, which standard classification misses, mainly for embankments, mineral seals and structures in contact with water: pinhole, double hydrometer, crumb and soluble salts in pore water (M.7).
sections.body: (1) The test identifies the dispersive character of clayey soil, which standard engineering classification does not; it is done on clayey soil mainly for earth embankments, mineral sealings and other structures in contact with water. (2) Four test types are considered (see M.7): the pinhole test, modelling water flowing along a crack; the double hydrometer test, comparing clay dispersion in plain water without stirring with that using a dispersant and mechanical stirring; the crumb test, observing soil crumbs in dilute sodium hydroxide; and soluble salts in pore water, relating sodium to total dissolved salts in a saturation extract. (p. 67)
key_points: Standard classification does not identify dispersive soil (p. 67).
Pinhole, double hydrometer, crumb and soluble salts tests (M.7) (p. 67).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Storage without drying, procedures and preparation are specified; results are linked to grading and consistency limits; pinhole compaction and mixing water are specified; a third hydrometer test or distilled water in the crumb test may be asked for.
sections.body: (1)P To be specified: storage so samples do not dry before testing, test procedures and specimen preparation. (2)P Results shall be linked to the sample's grading and consistency limits. (3) For the pinhole test, specimen compaction (e.g. wet or dry of optimum) and mixing water (e.g. distilled or reservoir) should be specified. (4) For the double hydrometer test, a third hydrometer test may be specified to study reservoir water's effect on the suspension. (5) For the crumb test, distilled water may be asked for besides the sodium hydroxide solution. (p. 67)
key_points: Do not let dispersibility samples dry before testing (p. 67).
Link results to grading and consistency limits (p. 67).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Frost susceptibility
sections.summary: Heading for frost susceptibility: objective (5.5.10.1), requirements (5.5.10.2) and evaluation (5.5.10.3).
sections.body: Heading for 5.5.10.1 to 5.5.10.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 68)
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: Frost susceptibility matters for foundations above the freezing front: roads, runways, railways, spread foundations, pipelines and dams can heave where frost-susceptible soil has water; risk may be estimated from classification properties or laboratory tests (M.8, X.5).
sections.body: (1) Frost susceptibility is essential to the design of foundations above the freezing front in frost-susceptible soil. (2) Roads, airport runways, railways, buildings on spread foundations, buried pipelines, dams and other structures can heave when frost-susceptible soil with access to water freezes; such soil may be natural or a constructed base. (3) Heave risk may be estimated from classification properties (grading, capillary rise and/or fines content) or from laboratory tests on natural, re-compacted and re-consolidated, or reconstituted samples. NOTE: see M.8 and X.5. (p. 68)
key_points: Frost heave affects roads, runways, railways, footings, pipelines, dams (p. 68).
Estimate risk from classification properties or laboratory tests (p. 68).
sections.applicability: The routine soil classification/identification/description test suite, performed in every phase of ground investigation.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Where classification does not clearly rule out heave (e.g. organic soil, peat, saline or artificial soil, widely graded coarse soil) laboratory frost heave tests are run, on natural samples for natural ground and re-compacted or reconstituted specimens for fill; CBR after thawing tests thaw weakening.
sections.body: (1) If classification does not clearly show no heave risk, laboratory frost heave tests should be run; soils needing them besides correlations include organic soil, peat, saline soil, artificial soil and coarse soil with a wide range of grain size. (2) Natural ground should be tested on natural samples; constructed fill on re-compacted then re-consolidated or reconstituted specimens. sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Some chemical constituents matter for durability; routine soil chemistry covers five tests only: organic content, carbonate content, sulfate content, pH and chloride content (Annex N); sulfide, magnesium, ammonium, resistivity and redox tests are not covered.
sections.body: (1) The detailed chemistry of soil is often of limited civil engineering interest, but some constituents can matter greatly, e.g. for durability of the structure (p. 68). (2) Routine soil laboratory chemistry is usually limited to organic content (loss on ignition, total organic content, organic matter), carbonate content, sulfate content, pH (acidity or alkalinity) and chloride content; only these five are dealt with. NOTE 1: Annex N gives detail and interpretation for each. NOTE 2: other constituents such as sulfide, magnesium and ammonium can make the ground very aggressive to steel and concrete; their testing is not covered. NOTE 3: corrosiveness to steel is usually judged from electrical resistivity and redox potential (not covered), pH, chlorides and sulfates (p. 69). (pp. 68 to 69)

Annex N details each chemical test (p. 69).

sections.body: (1)P To be specified for all chemical tests: the samples and their number; the test procedures; pre-treatments including treatment of oversize particles (i.e. D > 2 mm); tests per stratum and duplicate tests; separate tests for a mean value; reporting format; supplementary classification tests for each test or series. (2)P Mixing, riffling and quartering shall be followed strictly to avoid inconsistent results. (3) Disturbed samples may be used, but particle size and water content must represent the field (Quality Classes 1 to 3). (4) For organic content, only the particle size distribution need be representative (Quality Class 4). NOTE: Annex N gives recommended procedures. (p. 69)

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: Organic content classifies the soil, often by loss on ignition in soils with little clay or carbonate, or more specifically by mass loss under hydrogen peroxide (H2O2); organic matter lowers bearing capacity, raises compressibility and swell-shrink, gas causes settlement, and it harms road stabilisation.
sections.body: (1) Organic content classifies the soil. With little or no clay and carbonate it is often found from loss on ignition at a controlled temperature; other tests serve, e.g. mass loss on treatment with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), a more specific measure. (2) Organic matter can harm engineering behaviour: bearing capacity falls, compressibility and swelling and shrinkage potential rise; gas can cause large immediate settlements and affect laboratory consolidation coefficients and shear strength; it harms stabilisation of road soils and usually comes with low pH and sometimes sulfates harmful to foundations. (p. 70)

Organic matter lowers bearing capacity and raises compressibility (p. 70).

(2) Acid-soluble sulfate is the total sulfate content, distinct from water-soluble sulfate; which value is relevant matters. (3) Groundwater with dissolved sulfates, especially sodium and magnesium sulfates, can attack concrete and other materials in or on the ground, so soil and groundwater are classified by sulfate content to decide precautions. sections.summary: Strength tests set drained and/or undrained shear strength parameters: unconfined compression, UU triaxial, consolidated triaxial, and translational and ring shear box (for drained conditions); only fully saturated or dry soil is dealt with.
sections.body: (1) The tests set drained and/or undrained shear strength parameters. (2) Covered: unconfined compression; unconsolidated undrained triaxial compression; consolidated triaxial compression; translational shear box and torsional shear box (ring shear) (pp. 73-74). (3) Translational and ring shear tests should be used for drained conditions. NOTE: at quick strain rates, very low permeability clays may sometimes be taken as loaded undrained in both, giving an indication of undrained strength. (4) Only tests on fully saturated or dry soil are dealt with (p. 74). (pp. 73 to 74)

sections.title: General requirements
sections.summary: Clay, silt and organic soil are tested on Quality Class 1 samples; coarse silts and sands may be re-compacted or reconstituted to the design structure and density; test numbers, specimen choice, orientation, test type, stresses, rates, failure and acceptance criteria are specified; three or more tests at different normal stresses per sample; Class 2 disturbance is allowed for (Annex P).
sections.body: (1) Shear strength of clay, silt and organic soil should be found on undisturbed (Quality Class 1) samples; for some soils or purposes, reconstituted or remoulded specimens serve. (2) Coarse silts and sands may be re-compacted or reconstituted, by a method reproducing as closely as possible the structure and density relevant to the design. (3)P For such specimens, the composition, density and water content relevant to in-situ conditions and the preparation method shall be specified. (4)P To be evaluated or specified: number of tests; specimen locations in the samples; sample quality; preparation; orientation; test type; classification tests; consolidation stresses and increment times (if applicable); shearing rate; failure criteria; termination criteria (e.g. the strain at which to stop); acceptability criteria (e.g. saturation, scatter); measurement accuracy; presentation format; any procedure beyond an accepted standard. (5) A sample's shear strength should come from a set of three or more tests at different normal stresses. (6)P For a stratum's strength, the type of shearing, the preparation method and the need for more classification tests shall be considered (pp. 74-75). (7) For Quality Class 2 samples, disturbance effects should be considered in interpretation. NOTE: Annex P gives a guideline on minimum samples and tests per stratum and more on the tests and evaluation (p. 75). (pp. 74 to 75)

Re-compacted or reconstituted specimens for coarse silts and sands (p. 74).

sections.body: (1)P Where applicable, presentation shall include effective stress paths, Mohr circles, stress-strain curves, pore pressure-strain curves and pore pressure parameters. NOTE: linear extrapolation can give wrong strength values as the failure envelope is generally curved, especially at low normal stresses. (2)P The stress range of the strength parameters shall be given. (3) Where suitable, results from the different laboratory and in-situ methods should be compared. (4) The strain rate used should be considered. (5) Compression and direct shear tests give commonly accepted parameters for routine design methods, not necessarily for other analyses. (6) Unconfined and unconsolidated undrained compression tests need not represent in-situ undrained strength. (p. 75)

sections.summary: Consolidated triaxial tests use quality class 1 specimens; saturation method and criterion, back-pressure, pore pressure measurement and stress paths are specified; one consistency limit and grading per set; reports state test type, parameters, shearing rate, failure criterion and deviations; advanced tests per 2.4.2.3 (4) should be considered.
sections.body: (1)P Tests shall be on undisturbed specimens of quality class 1; NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-9 (X.4.4.3). (2)P Further to 5.8.2: saturation method and criterion, back-pressure, and any procedure beyond an accepted standard (e.g. lubricated ends, local strain or pore pressure measurement) (p. 76). (3)P For consolidated undrained tests, pore pressure measurement requirements and the total stress path for shearing shall be specified. (4)P For consolidated drained tests, the volume change device and the stress path shall be specified. (5)P Water content before and after and bulk density before shall be found for each specimen. (6) One consistency limit test and particle size analysis should be done per set of triaxial tests in a stratum. (7)P Results shall state the test type, the parameters given, the shearing rate and the failure criterion (e.g. peak deviator stress, maximum stress ratio). (8)P Known deviations from standard procedure (e.g. degree of saturation, procedures, specimen composition) shall be reported. (9) Per 2.4.2.3 (4), more advanced tests should be considered, such as triaxial extension, simple shear, plane strain compression and extension, true triaxial and directional shear, all possibly with anisotropic rather than isotropic consolidation (p. 77). (pp. 76 to 77)

State failure criterion, e.g. peak deviator stress or maximum stress ratio (p. 77).
Consider advanced tests with anisotropic consolidation (p. 77).

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: Undrained strength, pore pressure parameters and stress-strain relations suffer more from disturbance than drained parameters; reliable moduli need advanced tests (5.9); results give φ' and c' or cu for drained and undrained stability analyses (EN 1997-1:2004, Annex D).
sections.body: (1) Evaluation should allow that undrained shear strength, pore pressure parameters and stress-strain relationships are affected by disturbance more than drained strength parameters. NOTE: reliable moduli, especially for stiff soil, need advanced tests with accurate strain and axial force measurement (see 5.9). (2) By test type, drained or undrained strength follows: effective angle of shearing resistance (φ') and effective cohesion (c'), or undrained shear strength (cu). (3) These can be used in drained and undrained stability analyses. NOTE: see EN 1997-1:2004, Annex D. (p. 77)
key_points: Undrained values are more disturbance-sensitive than drained (p. 77).
Gives φ' and c' or cu for stability analyses (p. 77).

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Shear box tests use Quality Class 1 specimens located and oriented to match the field, failure being forced near the mid-height horizontal plane; shearing is slow enough to dissipate pore pressures, which cannot be measured.
sections.body: (1)P Tests shall be on undisturbed specimens of Quality Class 1; NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-10 (X.4.4.4) (p. 77). (2)P Location and orientation shall be chosen to match in-situ conditions as closely as possible; in translational and ring shear, failure is forced on or near a horizontal plane mid-specimen. (3)P Positive or negative shear-induced pore pressures shall be avoided, as they cannot be measured; shearing shall be slow enough for them to dissipate (p. 78). (pp. 77 to 78)

Failure forced near the mid-height horizontal plane (p. 78).

sections.summary: Heading for oedometer compressibility testing: objective (5.9.2.1), requirements (5.9.2.2) and evaluation and use (5.9.2.3).

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: The oedometer confines a cylindrical specimen laterally under load increments with axial drainage, or at constant rate of strain; incremental compression and swelling tests give compression, consolidation and swelling characteristics, and the collapse potential test gives unsaturated compressibility and added compression on inundation.
sections.body: (1) In the oedometer a laterally confined cylindrical specimen takes discrete increments of vertical loading or unloading and drains axially; compression and swelling tests and collapse potential are covered. (2) A continuous loading (constant rate of strain) test may be used instead. (3) Incremental compression and swelling tests determine compression, consolidation and swelling characteristics. (4) The collapse potential test sets compressibility parameters of the unsaturated soil and the extra compression on inundation from structural collapse. (p. 78)
key_points: Incremental loading or constant rate of strain (p. 78).
Collapse potential gives extra compression on inundation (p. 78).
sections.applicability: Laboratory determination of soil compressibility/stiffness parameters (Eoed, Cc, Cs) for settlement analysis.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Compressibility of clay, silt or organic soil uses Quality Class 1 samples (small strain moduli below 1 % strain are very disturbance-sensitive); the initial vertical stress does not exceed the in-situ vertical effective stress (one fourth of it for strain-softening clays); the top stress well exceeds the in-situ maximum; inundation stress for collapse matches the in-situ range (Annex Q).
sections.body: (1)P Quality Class 1 samples shall be used for compressibility of clay, silt or organic soil; NOTE: small strain moduli (e.g. below 1 % strain for soft to medium clays) are very sensitive to sampling, so per 3.4.3 (3)P specific methods such as block or stationary piston sampling may be used (p. 78). (2)P For re-compacted specimens, the composition, density and water content relevant to in-situ conditions and the preparation method shall be specified. (3)P To be considered: existing field investigation results; settlement records from neighbouring sites; number and quality of samples; number and type of field tests; sensitive and cemented samples; preparation; orientation; extra classification tests. (4) Alternatives such as constant rate of strain tests may be considered. (5)P The initial vertical stress shall not exceed the in-situ vertical effective stress; NOTE: for strain-softening clays, one fourth of the in-situ vertical effective stress can be suitable. (6) The highest compression stress should be well above the maximum in-situ effective vertical stress; swelling decrements should cover the in-situ stress range. (7)P Collapse specimens shall be chosen with knowledge of the soil's behaviour on inundation, and the inundation stress related to the in-situ vertical stress range. NOTE 1: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-5 (X.4.5). NOTE 2: Annex Q gives minimum samples and tests per stratum and more on the test (p. 79). (pp. 78 to 79)
key_points: Quality Class 1 samples for clay, silt and organic soil (p. 78).
Initial vertical stress not above in-situ vertical effective stress (p. 79).
One fourth of in-situ stress can suit strain-softening clays (p. 79).
Annex Q gives minimum numbers of tests per stratum (p. 79).
sections.applicability: Laboratory determination of soil compressibility/stiffness parameters (Eoed, Cc, Cs) for settlement analysis.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: Oedometer results estimate the yield stress (pre-consolidation pressure), strongly affected by disturbance; compressibility is characterised by Eoed, mv, Cc and σ'p, unloading by Cs; Cα gives creep settlement and cv comes from one-dimensional consolidation theory; these serve simple spread foundation settlement and, with sample methods (EN 1997-1:2004, F.1, F.2), Eoed.
sections.body: (1) Results may estimate the yield stress (pre-consolidation pressure) of clays, organic soil and silty soil. (2) The oedometer pre-consolidation pressure can be greatly affected by sampling disturbance. (3) The most common compressibility values are the oedometer modulus (Eoed), coefficient of compressibility (mv), compression index (Cc) and pre-consolidation pressure (σ'p); unloading and recompression can be represented by the swelling index (Cs); all come directly from the relevant parts of the test curves (p. 79). (4) Creep settlement can be computed with the coefficient of secondary compression (Cα). (5) The coefficient of consolidation cv can be derived from one-dimensional consolidation theory. (6) Any parameter in (3) can be used for simple settlement analyses of spread foundations. (7) With sample methods, the oedometer modulus may be used; NOTE: examples in EN 1997-1:2004, F.1 and F.2 (p. 80). (pp. 79 to 80)
key_points: Pre-consolidation pressure is strongly affected by disturbance (p. 79).
Eoed, mv, Cc, σ'p and Cs from the test curves (p. 79).
Cα for creep; cv from one-dimensional consolidation theory (p. 80).
Sample methods in EN 1997-1:2004, F.1 and F.2 (p. 80).

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: Triaxial deformability testing gives deformation moduli (stiffness), varying with loading path, drained E' or undrained Eu by drainage, and tangent or secant moduli at different stress or strain levels as soil is non-linear.
sections.body: (1) The test determines deformation moduli (stiffness parameters). (2) Various stiffnesses can be measured by loading path. (3) By drainage, drained E' or undrained Eu can be found. (4) As soil is non-linear, moduli such as tangent and/or secant may be defined at different stress or strain levels. (p. 80)
key_points: Drained E' or undrained Eu (p. 80).
Tangent or secant moduli at different strain levels (p. 80).
sections.applicability: Laboratory determination of soil compressibility/stiffness parameters (Eoed, Cc, Cs) for settlement analysis.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Stiffness of a stratum uses Quality Class 1 samples; strains below 0,1 % need high-resolution instrumentation, very small strain moduli shear wave or dynamic methods; sample quality, sensitivity, saturation, consolidation state, cementation, preparation and orientation are considered.
sections.body: (1)P Quality Class 1 samples shall be used for stratum stiffness; NOTE: small strain moduli (e.g. below 1 % strain) are very sensitive to sampling, so per 3.4.3 (3)P block or stationary piston sampling or similar may be used. (2)P Special high-resolution stress and strain instrumentation shall be used for stiffness at strains below 0,1 %; NOTE: very small strain moduli can come from shear wave propagation or other dynamic methods. (3)P To be considered: sample quality; sensitivity, saturation, consolidation state and cementation; preparation; orientation. (p. 80)
key_points: Quality Class 1 samples for stiffness (p. 80).
High-resolution instrumentation below 0,1 % strain (p. 80).
Shear wave or dynamic methods for very small strain moduli (p. 80).
sections.applicability: Laboratory determination of soil compressibility/stiffness parameters (Eoed, Cc, Cs) for settlement analysis.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: Stiffness is given as a full curve or conventional values such as initial Young's modulus E0 or E50 at 50 % of the maximum shear stress; for soft normally consolidated soil, standard triaxial strength tests may sometimes give it.
sections.body: (1) Stiffness may be given by a complete curve or by conventional values, e.g. the initial Young's modulus (E0) or E50 at 50 % of the maximum shear stress. (2) For soft normally consolidated soil, Young's modulus and stress-strain curves may sometimes come from standard triaxial strength tests (p. 81). (pp. 80 to 81)
key_points: E0 or E50 at 50 % of maximum shear stress (p. 81).
Standard triaxial tests may serve for soft normally consolidated soil (p. 81).

sections.body: (1)P To be specified or checked: handling of oversize fractions; treatment of stiff fine soil; specimen preparation and maturing; test procedures and compaction effort; whether moulds and rammers conform to the standard(s). (2) In-situ tests instead of laboratory tests should be considered for special soils. (p. 81)

sections.body: (1)P Compaction characteristics shall be reported with grading curves and the oversize proportion by dry mass, with correction if appropriate. (2) The optimum water content (wopt) and corresponding maximum dry density under the applied effort (ρd,max) can be used to judge compacted fill quality. (p. 81)

sections.title: California Bearing ratio (CBR) test
sections.summary: Heading for the California Bearing Ratio (CBR) test: objective (5.10.3.1), requirements (5.10.3.2) and evaluation and use (5.10.3.3).

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: The CBR of a compacted or undisturbed sample is the percentage of the standard load at the standard penetration of a standard cylindrical plunger.
sections.body: (1) The test determines the California Bearing Ratio (CBR) of a compacted or undisturbed sample (p. 81). (2) CBR is the percentage of the standard load matching the standard penetration when a cylindrical plunger of standard cross-section penetrates the soil (p. 82). (pp. 81 to 82)
key_points: CBR = percentage of standard load at standard penetration (p. 82).

sections.summary: CBR preparation, number of tests, oversize (D > 16 mm), maturing, soaking and swell, surcharge, compaction water content, dry density or effort, equipment conformity and one or both ends are specified or checked.
sections.body: (1)P To be specified or checked: preparation of each specimen; number of tests in a set; handling of oversize fractions (D > 16 mm); maturing; soaking or not, and swell measurement if soaked; surcharge for soaking and testing; water content for compacted specimens; dry density or compactive effort; equipment (moulds and rammers) conformity; testing one or both ends. Specify soaking, swell and surcharge (p. 82).

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: CBR results are reported with grading and oversize proportion; CBR is a basic flexible pavement design parameter and rates sub-grade, sub-base and base materials, recycled included, for roads, railways and airfields.
sections.body: (1)P Results shall be reported with grading and oversize proportion by dry mass, if relevant. (2) CBR can be a basic parameter for flexible pavement design and can rate the potential strength of sub-grade, sub-base and base course materials (including recycled) for road, railway and airfield pavements. (p. 82)

sections.title: Objective
sections.summary: The test sets the coefficient of permeability (hydraulic conductivity) for water flow through saturated soil.
sections.body: (1) The test sets the coefficient of permeability (hydraulic conductivity) for water flow through water-saturated soil. (p. 82)
key_points: Coefficient of permeability of saturated soil (p. 82).
sections.applicability: Laboratory determination of the coefficient of permeability (hydraulic conductivity) for seepage/drainage/consolidation analysis.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.summary: Test type, orientation and classification are considered; clay, silt and organic soil need stress conditions, steady-flow criterion, flow direction, gradient, back-pressure and fluid chemistry specified, sand and gravel density index, gradient and back-pressure; gradients stay near the field and within Darcy's law; Quality Classes 1 or 2 for fine soil, Class 3 or re-compacted for sand and gravel.
sections.body: (1)P To be considered: preferred test type, specimen orientation, extra classification tests; NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-11 (X.4.7). (2)P To be specified by use: a) in clay, silt and organic soil (p. 82): test stress conditions; criterion for reaching and keeping steady flow; flow direction; hydraulic gradient; back-pressure and degree of saturation; chemistry of the percolating fluid; b) in sand and gravel: density index of the specimen; hydraulic gradient; back-pressure and degree of saturation. (3) The laboratory gradient should be close to the field one unless a problem needs otherwise. (4)P Laboratory and in-situ gradients shall be checked to lie within Darcy's law. (5) Known deviations from standard procedure should be reported. (6) Only Quality Classes 1 or 2 should be used for clay, silt or organic soil. (7) For sand and gravel, Quality Class 3 and remoulded or re-compacted samples may be used. (8) Volume change from consolidation should affect the measured permeability only negligibly. NOTE: Annex S gives minimum samples and tests per stratum and more on the test (p. 83). (pp. 82 to 83)
key_points: Laboratory gradient close to field; within Darcy's law (p. 83).
Quality Classes 1 or 2 for clay, silt and organic soil (p. 83).
Quality Class 3 or re-compacted for sand and gravel (p. 83).
Annex S gives minimum numbers of tests per stratum (p. 83).
sections.applicability: Laboratory determination of the coefficient of permeability (hydraulic conductivity) for seepage/drainage/consolidation analysis.

sections.title: Evaluation and use of test results
sections.summary: Evaluation weighs how boundary conditions (saturation, flow direction, gradient, stress, density, layering, side leakage, filter head loss) affect results and match the field; partially saturated soil may be much less permeable; temperature correction is considered; k follows from Darcy's law and serves seepage, dewatering, sheet pile and seepage pressure design.
sections.body: (1) Evaluation should assess how far boundary conditions (degree of saturation, flow direction, gradient, stress, density and layering, side leakage and head loss in filter and tubing) affect results and how well they match the field. (2) For partially saturated soil, much smaller values than the saturated ones may be relevant. (3) A temperature correction should be considered. (4) The coefficient of permeability can be computed assuming Darcy's law holds (p. 83). (5) It can be used in designing excavations and earth dams to estimate seepage, to assess groundwater lowering, to design sheet pile walls, to estimate seepage pressures and so on (p. 84). (pp. 83 to 84)
key_points: Check boundary conditions against the field (p. 83).
Partially saturated soil may be much less permeable (p. 83).
k used for seepage, dewatering and sheet pile design (p. 84).

sections.summary: Rock classification results are reviewed together with drilling and geophysical logs, core photographs and experience, compared with geology to build an engineering geological model, guided by geological maps, with second opinions if needed for consistency.
sections.body: (1)P Results shall be reviewed together and compared with drilling logs, geophysical logs, core photographs and comparable experience. (2) Soil and rock classification should be compared with the geological background to give an engineering geological model. (3) Geological maps should guide rock and rock mass classification where available. (4) Second opinions and typical examples with rock comparisons may be needed for a consistent description. (p. 84)

sections.summary: Rock material and mass are identified and described by mineralogy, grain size, genetic group, structure and weathering per EN ISO 14689-1, on cores, samples or in situ; more detailed description specifies the system, analyses and format; every sample received is described.
sections.body: (1) Identification and description of rock material and mass rest on mineralogical composition, predominant grain size, genetic group, structure, weathering and other components, on cores, other samples or rock masses in situ. (2)P The laboratory procedure shall conform to EN ISO 14689-1. (3) Where more detailed description is used, specify the classification system, any advanced geological analyses and the reporting format (p. 84). (4) All samples received should be identified and described whatever their homogeneity, as this frames all testing and evaluation (p. 85). (pp. 84 to 85)

Describe every sample received (p. 85).

sections.summary: Rock mass classification from cores needs the highest possible core recovery to find discontinuities and cavities, and drilling disturbance is evaluated since quality designations rest on core fractures.
sections.body: (1) Rock mass classification from cores should rest on the highest possible core recovery to identify discontinuities and possible cavities. (2) Drilling disturbance of the core should be evaluated, as most rock mass quality designations depend on core fractures and their quality. (p. 85)

Evaluate drilling disturbance of cores (p. 85).

sections.summary: Heading for rock water content determination: objective and requirements (5.12.4.1) and evaluation (5.12.4.2).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Rock water content is found by oven-drying at (105 ± 5) °C except as in 5.12.4.2 (2), on at least 50 g or a core piece at least 10 times the maximum grain size; water retention, storage, re-saturation and test numbers are specified; reports say whether it is the in-situ value (U.3, X.4.9.2).
sections.body: (1)P Except for the rocks in 5.12.4.2 (2), rock water content shall be found by oven-drying at (105 ± 5) °C. (2)P Measures to retain water in sampling and storage shall be specified if relevant. (3)P To be specified: sample selection; laboratory storage; possible vacuum re-saturation of desiccated samples; tests per stratum; parallel tests on the same formation; accuracy checks. (4) A sample of at least 50 g, or a core piece at least 10 times the maximum mineral grain size, should be used. (5)P The report shall state whether the value is the in-situ water content. NOTE: with no ISO/CEN rock standard yet, the methods in U.3 with X.4.9.2 can be applied. (p. 85)

At least 50 g or 10 times the maximum grain size (p. 85).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Water contents are compared with saturated values for the density or porosity and anomalies retested; gypsum-bearing rock is dried at 50 °C since bound water may dehydrate at 105 °C; dissolved salts and closed pores are allowed for; water content correlates strength and deformation.
sections.body: (1) Water contents should be compared with the fully saturated value for the specimen's density (or porosity); anomalies should be retested. (2) Rock with significant gypsum should be tested at 50 °C, as bound water may partly dehydrate at 105 °C. (3) For rock whose pore water holds dissolved salts, or with closed pores, the reported value should be evaluated accordingly. (4) Water content should be used to correlate strength and deformation of rock types in boreholes and at test sites (p. 85). (5) Comparisons with available water content and rock type correlations should be made (p. 86). (pp. 85 to 86)
key_points: Compare with saturated water content; retest anomalies (p. 85).
Gypsum-bearing rock at 50 °C, not 105 °C (p. 85).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Bulk and dry density from weighing and a reliable volume give porosity, the ratio of pore volume to total volume, using particle density as for soil if no closed pores exist; specimens of at least 50 g and 10 times the maximum grain size (U.4, X.4.9.3).
sections.body: (1) The test gives bulk and dry density, from weight analysis with a reliable sample volume, to obtain porosity and related properties. (2) Pore volume may be computed from dry density and particle density found as for soil, if the specimen has no closed pores; porosity is pore volume over total volume. (3)P To be specified: sample selection; storage; whether and how desiccated samples are re-saturated; tests per formation; parallel tests on the same formation. (4) Specimens of at least 50 g with a minimum dimension of 10 times the maximum mineral grain size should be tested. NOTE: with no ISO/CEN rock standard yet, the methods in U.4 with the bibliography in X.4.9.3 can be applied. (p. 86)
key_points: Porosity = pore volume / total volume (p. 86).
At least 50 g and 10 times the maximum grain size (p. 86).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Density and porosity are reported with the rock description and strength and deformation characteristics and used for correlations; closed pores affect porosity, so total pore volume uses the solid density of a powdered sample (CEN ISO/TS 17892-3, X.4.9.3).
sections.body: (1) Density and porosity should be integrated in reporting the rock description and strength and deformation characteristics in boreholes and at test sites. (2) They should be used to compare strength and deformation properties and build correlations per rock type. (3) Closed pores can affect porosity; total pore volume should use the density of solids of a powdered sample. NOTE: see CEN ISO/TS 17892-3 (X.4.9.3). (p. 86)

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Three swelling tests are covered: swelling pressure index at zero volume change, swelling strain index of radially confined specimens under axial surcharge, and unconfined swelling strain; mainly for clay-rich rocks such as claystone and shale; disintegrating rocks get soil classification tests (Annex V).
sections.body: (1) Tests for swelling potential under wetting and drying or unloading in water: the swelling pressure index at zero volume change; the swelling strain index for radially confined specimens with axial surcharge (p. 86); and the swelling strain of unconfined specimens. NOTE: rocks with high clay content in particular can swell, weaken and disintegrate; the index tests indicate swelling under controlled conditions, usually on softer rocks like claystone and shale, and can characterise harder rocks subject to weathering. (2) Rocks that disintegrate should be further classified with soil tests such as shrinkage, liquid and plastic limits, grading and clay mineral type and content. NOTE: Annex V gives detail and interpretation (p. 87). (pp. 86 to 87)
key_points: Three swelling tests: pressure index, confined strain index, unconfined strain (p. 86).
Usually on claystone and shale (p. 87).
Annex V details the swelling tests (p. 87).

sections.title: General requirements
sections.summary: Swelling specimens follow recommended practice for right cylinders or rectangular prisms (X.4.8), with one swell axis perpendicular to bedding or foliation; samples, preparation, numbers, method, water, recording period, time curves and reporting are specified.
sections.body: (1) Specimens should closely follow recommended practice for right cylinders or rectangular prisms, the sample allowing re-coring and/or lathe machining with one swell measurement axis perpendicular to bedding or foliation. NOTE: see X.4.8. (2)P To be specified: sample selection; preparation, orientation and dimensions; tests per formation; method, equipment and calibration; water (natural or distilled, chemistry); recording period; need for swell pressure or displacement curves against time since flooding; additional parameters; reporting. (p. 87)

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Swelling results are reviewed with the description to set classification parameters and compared with field experience of comparable rock; laboratory tests may only partly reflect long-term swelling, weakening and disintegration because of fissuring, stress, drainage and pore water chemistry.
sections.body: (1)P Results shall be reviewed against the description and classification parameters set. (2) Design values from laboratory tests should be compared with field experience of comparable rock under similar climate, loading and wetting. (3) Short and especially long term swelling, weakening or disintegration under wetting and drying may be only partly reflected by laboratory tests, owing among others to natural fissuring, stress, drainage and pore water chemistry. (p. 87)

Laboratory tests only partly reflect long-term weathering (p. 87).

sections.body: (1) The test measures the pressure needed to keep an undisturbed rock specimen at constant volume when immersed. (2) It may estimate in-situ swell pressure by comparison with documented experience for the stratum. (3)P Specimens shall be cored by Category A sampling methods. NOTE: see V.2. (pp. 87 to 88)

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: The force is corrected for test cell deformation; the maximum swell pressure at zero volume change is an upper limit under laboratory conditions, and field evidence on weathering, loading, water content and pore water chemistry is weighed before design use.
sections.body: (1)P The force for zero volume change shall be corrected for deformation of the cell itself (ball bearings and bedding of filter stones against the end platens). (2) The maximum swell pressure at zero volume change should be used as an upper limit under the specified laboratory conditions. (3) Before design use, field evidence on short and especially long term weathering by wetting and drying, loading, water content and pore water chemistry should be considered. (p. 88)

sections.body: (1) The test measures axial swelling strain against a constant axial surcharge when a radially confined undisturbed specimen is immersed. (2)P Specimens shall be cored by Category A sampling methods. NOTE: see V.3. (p. 88)

sections.summary: Strain is corrected for test cell deformation; axial swelling strain estimates in-situ swell potential with documented experience and, by vertical stress, informs heave or lateral deformation at a rock-structure interface.
sections.body: (1)P Measured strain shall be corrected for deformation of the cell itself (ball bearings and bedding of filter stones against the end platens). (2) Axial swelling strain under constant surcharge should estimate in-situ swell potential, using documented experience for the stratum. (3) Depending on the vertical stress, the test supports evaluation of vertical heave or lateral deformation at a rock/structure interface. (p. 88)

sections.summary: The test measures swelling strain of an unconfined undisturbed rock specimen in water, only on specimens from at least category B methods that keep their shape; slaking, less durable rocks get a confined test; the report states no radial confinement (V.4).
sections.body: (1) The test measures swelling strain of an unconfined undisturbed specimen immersed in water. (2)P Only for specimens from at least category B sampling methods that do not change shape appreciably in testing. (3) Slaking, less durable rocks should be tested with a confined swelling test. NOTE: see V.4. (4)P The report shall state clearly that the specimen was not radially confined. (p. 89)

sections.summary: Unconfined swelling strain estimates in-situ swell potential by comparison with documented experience, and strains and directions relative to bedding or foliation are only an estimate.
sections.body: (1) The test may estimate in-situ swell potential by comparison with documented experience for the stratum. (2) Unconfined strains and their directions relative to bedding or foliation should be used only as an estimate of in-situ swelling potential. (p. 89)

sections.body: (1) Five methods: uniaxial compression and deformability; point load; direct shear; Brazil; triaxial compression. NOTE: Annex W details each and its interpretation. (p. 89)

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Rock strength results are screened against recognised databases, allowing for natural range and classification correlations, grouped by geology and classification with statistics, and used for in-situ properties and rock element and mass classification.
sections.body: (1) Evaluation should compare results with recognised databases to screen anomalies, allowing for the natural range of compressive strength and deformation parameters in rock and for correlations with classification tests. (2) All results should be grouped and analysed by geological description and classification properties, statistically where suitable. (3) Values can be used to evaluate in-situ strength and deformation and to classify rock element and rock mass properties. (p. 90)

Group by geology; use statistics where suitable (p. 90).

sections.summary: Heading for the uniaxial compression and deformability test: objective and requirements (5.14.4.1) and evaluation (5.14.4.2).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Uniaxial compression measures compressive strength, Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio of cylindrical rock specimens for intact rock classification; orientation, dimensions, method and modulus definition are specified; specimens come from Category A cores (Annex W).
sections.body: (1) The test measures compressive strength, Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio of cylindrical specimens. (2) It serves classification and characterisation of intact rock. (3)P Besides 5.14.2: specimen orientation and dimensions; method; where relevant, the definition of modulus (tangent, average or secant) and Poisson's ratio as a function of stress or strain. (4)P Specimens shall be from cores taken by Category A sampling. (5) Recommendations for the test should be followed. NOTE: see Annex W. (p. 90)
key_points: Strength, Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio of intact rock (p. 90).
Category A cores (p. 90).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Uniaxial strength is the maximum vertical stress; modulus is tangent at a fixed percentage (i.e. 50 %), mean over the linear part, or secant to a fixed percentage; Poisson's ratio is the slope of radial versus axial strain over the same stress interval; σc classifies intact rock and with triaxial results gives φ and c.
sections.body: (1) Uniaxial compressive strength should be the maximum vertical stress in the test. (2) The modulus, axial stress change over the axial strain it produces, should use one of: tangent modulus at a fixed percentage of ultimate strength (i.e. 50 %); mean modulus over the linear part of the stress-strain curve; secant modulus from zero to a fixed percentage of ultimate strength (i.e. 50 %) (p. 90). (3) Poisson's ratio should be the slope of radial strain against axial strain. (4) Modulus and Poisson's ratio should be computed over the same vertical stress interval. (5) Results should be evaluated against classification and the rupture pattern, sketched. (6) The unconfined compressive strength (σc) can classify intact rock and, with triaxial results in a Mohr diagram, define the Mohr-Coulomb parameters angle of shearing resistance (φ) and cohesion (c). NOTE: E and ν may be used for settlement per EN 1997-1:2004, Annex F (p. 91). (pp. 90 to 91)
key_points: Strength = maximum vertical stress (p. 90).
Tangent, mean or secant modulus, at 50 % where fixed (p. 90).
Poisson's ratio = slope of radial vs axial strain (p. 91).
E and ν for settlement per EN 1997-1:2004, Annex F (p. 91).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: The point load test is a strength index test for rock classification, not a direct strength measure, with its strength correlation documented each time; methods for cores, blocks and lumps are specified; Category A cores, or Category B blocks and lumps from pits if reported (W.2).
sections.body: (1) The test is a strength index test for classifying rock, and can estimate strength for a group of rocks of the same competence range. (2) It is an index, not a direct strength measure; its correlation with strength should be documented each time. (3)P Besides 5.14.2 (1)P, methods for cores, blocks and irregular lumps shall be specified. (4)P Specimens shall be from Category A cores. (5) Blocks and irregular lumps from pits may be used if so reported and taken by Category B sampling. (6) Recommendations should be followed. NOTE: see W.2. (p. 91)
key_points: Point load is an index, not a direct strength test (p. 91).
Document the strength correlation each time (p. 91).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Point load results are treated statistically: of at least 10 tests, the two highest and two lowest are dropped before averaging; classing by mean index needs at least five tests; the test gives the Point Load Strength Index and the Strength Anisotropy Index.
sections.body: (1)P Given the large variability, characterisation and prediction of other strength parameters shall be statistical: from at least 10 single tests, delete the two highest and two lowest values and average the rest. (2) Classing samples or strata by a mean Point Load Strength Index should use at least five tests (p. 91). (3) The test measures the Point Load Strength Index and the Strength Anisotropy Index, the ratio of the point load strengths in the directions giving the greatest and least values (p. 92). (pp. 91 to 92)
key_points: At least 10 tests; drop two highest and two lowest (p. 91).
At least five tests to class by mean index (p. 91).
Strength Anisotropy Index = greatest / least point load strength (p. 92).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Direct shear measures peak and residual shear strength against normal stress, giving basic shear parameters and the surface characteristics of a controlling discontinuity, described for joint type, roughness, filling and water; machine, rate and normal stresses are specified; Category A cores or Category B pit blocks (W.3).
sections.body: (1) The test measures peak and residual shear strength against normal stress on the shear plane. (2) It covers basic shear strength parameters and surface characteristics of a controlling discontinuity. (3) Where those are determined, the description should give joint type and roughness, filling type and thickness, and water in the joint. (4)P Besides 5.14.2 (1)P: orientation and dimensions; machine specification; shear displacement rate; normal stresses for the single tests. (5)P Specimens shall be from Category A cores or from pit blocks taken by at least Category B sampling. (6) Recommendations should be followed. NOTE: see W.3. (p. 92)
key_points: Peak and residual shear strength versus normal stress (p. 92).
Describe joint roughness, filling and water (p. 92).
sections.applicability: The definitive rock-strength laboratory test suite, feeding Mohr-Coulomb and point-load-index strength parameters into rock foundation, slope, and excavation design.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Evaluation studies the shear plane for bedding, schistosity, cleavage or rock-concrete interface; φ and c come from several specimens by Mohr-Coulomb, residual values from repeated normal stresses on one plane; the forced plane is usually along a known discontinuity; use needs geological correlation.
sections.body: (1) Evaluation should study the shear plane, allowing for bedding and schistosity, cleavage, the rock-concrete interface or whatever was tested. (2) Angle of shearing resistance (φ) and cohesion (c) may be set from shear tests on several specimens of a stratum by the Mohr-Coulomb criterion; residual values from multiple tests at different normal stresses on an established rupture plane. (3) The test measures shear strength on a forced rupture plane under set normal stresses, giving peak and residual strength; usually the plane follows a known discontinuity. (4) It serves strength classification and characterisation of intact rock and should not be used without geological correlation and rock classification for field conditions. (p. 92)
key_points: φ and c by Mohr-Coulomb from several specimens (p. 92).
Residual values by repeated normal stresses on one plane (p. 92).
Not without geological correlation (p. 92).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: The Brazil test measures indirectly the uniaxial tensile strength of a cylindrical rock specimen; duplicate parallel-cut specimens are tested; anisotropic rock is cut parallel and perpendicular to bedding with load direction stated; Category A cores (W.4).
sections.body: (1) The test measures indirectly the uniaxial tensile strength of a cylindrical specimen. (2)P Besides 5.14.2 (1)P: orientation and dimensions; method. (3)P Given the variability, duplicate tests on specimens cut in parallel shall be done. (4) For shales and other anisotropic rock, cut specimens parallel and perpendicular to bedding, stating load direction relative to bedding for parallel cuts. (5)P Specimens shall be from Category A cores. (6) Recommendations should be followed. NOTE: see W.4. (p. 93)

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Hidden weakness planes may disturb the result, so the failure plane is sketched; the test gives tensile strength σT on a forced plane, which classifies intact rock and with compression Mohr circles defines φ and c; use needs geological correlation.
sections.body: (1) Hidden weakness planes may disturb the result; the failure plane should be sketched and evaluated. (2) The test gives an indirect tensile strength σT on a forced rupture plane. (3) σT may classify intact rock and, at a corresponding maximal stress σ1 with Mohr circles from uniaxial or triaxial tests, define the Mohr-Coulomb angle of shearing resistance (φ) and cohesion (c). (4) It serves strength classification and characterisation of intact rock; results should not be used without geological correlation and rock classification for field conditions. (p. 93)

σT with compression Mohr circles defines φ and c (p. 93).

sections.title: Objective and requirements
sections.summary: Triaxial compression of cylindrical rock specimens gives the Mohr-Coulomb envelope, angle of shearing resistance and cohesion intercept; drainage and pore pressure are usually not provided, though in shales, porous limestone and chalk advanced systems are needed; Category A cores (W.5).
sections.body: (1) The test measures strength of cylindrical specimens in triaxial compression; several tests give the Mohr-Coulomb envelope, and from it the angle of shearing resistance and cohesion intercept. NOTE: drainage and pore pressure measurement are usually not provided; in some rocks (e.g. shales, porous limestone and chalk) pore pressure may affect results, needing advanced systems measuring pore pressure and volumetric strain, possibly with techniques as for uniaxial strength per W.1. (2)P Besides 5.14.2 (1)P, orientation and dimensions reflecting the method shall be specified. (3)P Specimens shall be from Category A cores. (4) Recommendations should be followed. NOTE: see W.5. (p. 94)

Shales, porous limestone and chalk may need pore pressure measurement (p. 94).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: A triaxial series at different confining pressures gives φ and c; specimen homogeneity is judged from geology and classification; parameters are for intact rock and need upscaling to the rock mass.
sections.body: (1) A triaxial test is a series of compression tests at different confining pressures; the envelope of confining pressure against axial stress at rupture gives the Mohr-Coulomb angle of shearing resistance (φ) and cohesion (c). (2) Homogeneity of the specimen series should be judged from the geological description and classification parameters. (3) The parameters relate to intact rock; in-situ values need upscaling from intact element tests to rock mass properties. (p. 94)
